Now I'm working out concrete expected values for the test, like verifying that "Hello, World!" encodes to a known Base64 string I can check decoding against.

I'm second-guessing whether Commons Codec appends a trailing line separator by default, since the chunk size and CRLF behavior aren't fully clear to me — safer to avoid asserting an exact encoded string and instead test decode-then-encode round-trip behavior.

Actually, the Base64InputStream Javadoc does explicitly document the default line length of 76 and CRLF line ending, so I can rely on that documented behavior rather than guessing. Since 13 bytes encode to only 20 base64 characters, well under 76, there's no line break inserted in this case.

To reduce risk, I think it's safer to design tests around round-tripping -- encoding then decoding with the same classes to verify consistency -- rather than relying on hardcoded literal output values, since I don't have direct access to the encoder's source.

For decoding, testing against a known valid base64 literal string is fine since decoding is deterministic per the standard alphabet. Now I want to map out all the branches to cover in read(byte[], int, int): null array throwing NullPointerException, negative offset or length throwing IndexOutOfBoundsException, offset exceeding array length, and offset+len exceeding array length.

I'm also planning cases for len==0 returning immediately, the initial read path where the buffer optimization kicks in when buffer size equals len versus when it doesn't, and the EOF case where the underlying stream returns immediately. Then I need to cover both the encode and decode branches, plus the case where base64 already has buffered data from a prior small read so it skips straight to reading results.

For the small-chunk read scenario, calling read with tiny lengths repeatedly on a longer stream is trickier since the first call can pull and decode a much larger chunk than requested from the underlying stream, leaving surplus decoded bytes buffered internally for subsequent calls to consume without hitting the underlying stream again.

I want to confirm this hasData() branch is naturally exercised by any multi-byte content test that reads one byte at a time, and I should double-check markSupported returns false as well.

I also need a helper to read an entire stream fully into a byte array by looping over single-byte reads until reaching -1, plus set up a stream instance for the boundary exception tests.

I should add a test with a throwing underlying InputStream to confirm IOException propagates correctly, and another test verifying the lineLength/lineSeparator constructor still allows proper decode/encode round-tripping since those params are ignored in decode mode.

This goes beyond the given class but is necessary since the stream depends on it, so I'll note that in comments. I don't think overflow scenarios with extreme offset/length values need testing, but I should check behavior on repeated reads after EOF is reached.

I'm sketching out the full test list now: constructor defaults, decoding a known string, round-trip encode/decode, custom line length and separator handling, single-byte reads at EOF and normally, null array and negative offset exceptions, and partial buffer reads where the array is larger than the requested length.

I'm rounding out the list with tests for zero-length reads, mark support being false, IOException propagation, repeated EOF reads, and non-Base64 character handling. I'm writing helper methods to fully read bytes from a Base64InputStream, one that reads byte-by-byte and another that reads in bulk chunks, both accumulating into a ByteArrayOutputStream so I can verify both read paths produce identical results.

I'm now thinking through which test cases exercise the optimization branch where the buffer length exactly matches the remaining length versus when it doesn't, since that distinction determines which code path gets triggered — I'm drafting a test where the buffer is larger than the requested length to confirm the partial-read branch behaves correctly.

I should also think through branch coverage for the combined conditions checking negative offset/length and out-of-bounds offset, making sure to test each side of the OR conditions separately: negative offset with valid length, negative length with valid offset, and offset exceeding buffer length.

For the actual test logic, I'm confirming both branches (buffer length equal to len, and buffer length differing from len) will produce correct decoded output through functional round-trip verification, even though the internal optimization itself isn't directly observable -- what matters is exercising both code paths for coverage. I'm also verifying that since test data is small, a single read call against the ByteArrayInputStream will pull in all available bytes at once, so the behavior stays predictable across both cases.

Still, I'm considering adding an optional test with a custom InputStream that deliberately returns 0 on the first call to exercise that specific branch and confirm the surrounding logic handles it correctly.
